title: Helio Bank - Security review: audit logging + SIEM export (Private)
summary: Helio Bank security review focused on Redwood audit log schema coverage for sensitive actions, field semantics (actor/impersonation, source IP, request/trace IDs), retention/residency, and SIEM export options for Private deployments. Redwood clarified delivery semantics (at-least-once with potential duplicates) and recommended dedupe using event_id. Customer asked for parity across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and for a mapping to SOC 2 / ISO-aligned controls. Next steps include sharing schema v1 + field dictionary, SIEM exporter configuration examples (Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel), and confirming Private parity timeline for a short list of admin workflows (RBAC changes, API key lifecycle, retention/residency config, export destination changes).
topics: Audit log event schema v1: required fields and taxonomy
Actor attribution: user vs service vs impersonation
Event delivery semantics and deduplication strategy
Retention period and data residency behavior in Private
SIEM export targets: Splunk HEC, Azure Sentinel/Log Analytics
Private deployment parity for sensitive actions and upgrade/install events
questions: Do audit events include the source IP and user agent for Console/admin actions?
How do you represent impersonation (support or admin acting on behalf of a tenant user)?
What is the retention default and can we configure it to 365 days in Private?
Are exports near-real-time and what happens during outages (buffering/retry)?
How do we dedupe duplicates if the exporter retries?
Can we get a control mapping / evidence pointers for SOC 2 and ISO 27001?
action_items: Redwood (Naomi Feldman) - Share audit log schema v1 + field dictionary and redaction guidance - Due 2026-01-17
Redwood (Kevin Osei) - Send Splunk HEC + Azure Sentinel Private exporter configuration examples (auth, batching, retry) - Due 2026-01-20
Redwood (Markus Klein) - Provide sample events for: RBAC role change, API key rotation, export destination update, retention/residency change - Due 2026-01-20
Helio (Dana Whitfield / Miguel Santos) - Confirm preferred ingestion format and required fields for SOC correlation (host, sourcetype/table, index/workspace) - Due 2026-01-22
Redwood (Liam O'Rourke) - Coordinate follow-up review with Helio SOC to validate sample events in Splunk/Sentinel - Due 2026-01-24
next_steps: Redwood to email schema v1 + event taxonomy names used for sensitive actions and note backcompat/versioning approach.
Redwood to provide Private SIEM exporter setup snippets for Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel (Log Analytics), including expected retry semantics and recommended dedupe configuration.
Helio to test sample events in a non-prod SIEM workspace and confirm any field renames/normalization needed for their correlation rules.
Schedule a 45-min technical follow-up focused on Private parity gaps and rollout timeline, plus evidence mapping for GRC.
transcript_text:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-16
Start time: 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Call type: Security review

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Kevin Osei (Security Eng - SIEM/export), Naomi Feldman (PM - Security & Compliance)
Helio Bank: Dana Whitfield (Security Eng), Miguel Santos (SOC Lead), Priya Desai (GRC), Ethan Chen (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer evaluating Redwood Private; audit logs and SIEM export are procurement blockers.
- Discussed audit event fields (actor, source_ip, correlation IDs), retention, and export reliability.
- Redwood explained schema v1, event taxonomy for sensitive actions, and dedupe guidance.

Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, looks like we’ve got Dana, Miguel, Priya, Ethan. Hey everyone. Thanks for making time. Goal today is audit logging and SIEM export for Private, and make sure we answer the questionnaire items.

[00:14] Dana Whitfield: Yep. Thanks, Liam. We’re basically trying to close out our security review. Audit logs are the big one. We need to understand what fields you capture, how long you retain, and if we can export to Splunk and/or Sentinel.

[00:28] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. I pulled in Naomi who owns security and compliance product-wise, and Kevin who’s closer to the exporter work. Markus is here for private architecture.

[00:38] Naomi Feldman: Hi all.

[00:40] Kevin Osei: Hey.

[00:41] Markus Klein: Hello.

[00:45] Miguel Santos: Hi. I’m Miguel, I run SOC. I’ll be picky about event fields.

[00:49] Liam O'Rourke: We love picky.

[00:52] Naomi Feldman: Same.

[00:55] Dana Whitfield: Cool. First question: what’s your audit log schema? Like, literally what fields. Actor, target, IP, timestamp, correlation IDs. We don’t want a random blob.

[01:10] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We’re standardizing on a canonical schema, versioned. At a high level: event_id, occurred_at, event_type, actor fields, target/resource fields, tenant context, and correlation IDs.

[01:25] Dana Whitfield: When you say actor fields, what exactly?

[01:28] Naomi Feldman: Actor is modeled as type + identifiers. So actor_type is typically user, service, or system. actor_id is like our internal principal ID, plus actor_email when available for a human. For Console actions, it’s the signed-in user. For API calls, it’s the key owner if we can resolve, plus the key id.

[01:50] Miguel Santos: Do you include source IP?

[01:52] Kevin Osei: For gateway and console-backed admin actions, yes: source_ip. Also user_agent when it’s coming from browser flows. For service-to-service events inside private, it’s trickier because it might be pod-to-pod. But we still stamp the request origin when it comes through the API gateway.

[02:13] Ethan Chen: In Private, our gateway is NGINX in front of your control plane. So you’ll get the X-Forwarded-For chain? Or are you taking the first hop?

[02:24] Kevin Osei: Good question. We take the client IP as configured by your proxy headers. In the private installer defaults we recommend honoring X-Forwarded-For but with an allowlist of trusted proxies so it’s not spoofed.

[02:40] Miguel Santos: That’s good. But we’ll want to see it spelled out. Also do you store the full forwarded chain or just the resolved client_ip?

[02:48] Kevin Osei: Today we store a normalized source_ip and optionally source_ip_chain as a string. But we cap length, because cardinality and payload size. We can talk about what you need.

[03:02] Priya Desai: And retention. What’s retained where, and for how long?

[03:07] Naomi Feldman: For Private, you control retention because the primary store is in your environment. Redwood components emit events and they go into the audit pipeline you run. We have defaults—like 90 days in the packaged stack—but you can configure longer. The main constraints are storage cost and index cost in SIEM.

[03:28] Priya Desai: We typically require 365 days for certain admin actions.

[03:32] Markus Klein: That’s doable in Private. The stack uses your backing storage (depending on whether you’re deploying with our bundled object store / OpenSearch or pointing it at your own). You can set index lifecycle policies.

[03:48] Dana Whitfield: Okay. But in Hosted, do you retain? Because we have both a Private pilot and a Hosted sandbox.

[03:54] Naomi Feldman: Hosted has platform retention defaults—shorter—because we push customers to export to their SIEM for long-term retention. We can share the current numbers for enterprise tiers. But since you’re evaluating Private, you’ll have more control.

[04:10] Miguel Santos: If I’m honest, I don’t care about hosted retention as long as export works reliably.

[04:15] Liam O'Rourke: Understood.

[04:17] Dana Whitfield: Next question: coverage. What do you consider “sensitive actions”? And is it complete for Private?

[04:24] Naomi Feldman: Our definition includes RBAC changes, credential lifecycle (API keys, tokens, SSO settings), policy/routing updates, retention/residency configuration, audit export configuration, and Private install/upgrade operations.

[04:41] Dana Whitfield: Good list. Do you have it enumerated as event types?

[04:45] Naomi Feldman: Yes, event taxonomy is enumerated, and we lint against it so teams can’t invent a random event name. That’s part of how we get to 100% coverage.

[04:59] Miguel Santos: “100%” is a bold claim.

[05:02] Naomi Feldman: Fair. We define 100% as: every sensitive action in that list must emit an audit event with required fields. We measure expected vs observed via telemetry. For Private, parity is a key workstream, because historically some installer actions weren’t emitting.

[05:22] Ethan Chen: Like upgrades and rollbacks?

[05:24] Markus Klein: Exactly. Install, upgrade, rollback, config apply, credential rotation in the installer are all being instrumented.

[05:34] Dana Whitfield: We actually had a bad experience with another vendor where private mode had half the events.

[05:40] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah, we hear that a lot. That’s why we’re standardizing.

[05:45] Miguel Santos: Can you give an example event? Like RBAC role change. What does it look like?

[05:51] Kevin Osei: Conceptually: event_type “rbac.role.updated” (name is close, may be “rbac.role.update” depending on registry). It includes actor_type=user, actor_id, actor_email, source_ip, target_type=role, target_id, plus a change_summary field. We don’t include the full before/after JSON if it’s huge, we include a diff summary that’s bounded.

[06:20] Dana Whitfield: Do you include the tenant and project?

[06:23] Naomi Feldman: Yes. tenant_id required, and project_id when scoped. We also include deployment_mode (hosted/dedicated/private) so you can filter.

[06:35] Miguel Santos: Correlation IDs. We need to tie the audit event to the API request in our reverse proxy logs and also your app logs. Do you have request id and trace id?

[06:46] Kevin Osei: Yes: request_id and trace_id. For Console-admin flows we also have an admin_action_id that stays stable across multi-step operations.

[06:58] Miguel Santos: Good. Is request_id an actual header we can capture? Like X-Request-Id?

[07:03] Markus Klein: In Private, you can configure the gateway to pass through or generate one. Our services propagate it. If you already have one, we’ll reuse.

[07:14] Dana Whitfield: Impersonation. Do you do support impersonation? And if yes how is that captured.

[07:20] Liam O'Rourke: We very rarely do it, but there are break-glass scenarios.

[07:23] Naomi Feldman: We model it explicitly. actor is the actual principal performing the action, and we have an impersonated_actor field as a string descriptor when support is acting on behalf of someone. Also an auth_context field string that indicates “impersonation=true” with a reason code. We can share the exact naming.

[07:48] Priya Desai: From a controls perspective we need evidence that any elevated access is audited.

[07:53] Naomi Feldman: Agreed. That’s one of the required event types in the taxonomy.

[08:01] Miguel Santos: Export. Let’s talk SIEM. We do Splunk Cloud primarily, HEC ingestion. Secondary is Microsoft Sentinel. Do you support both?

[08:11] Kevin Osei: Yes. Splunk HEC is supported with batching and backoff. Sentinel via Log Analytics / Data Collector API is supported as well. We also can do generic HTTPS.

[08:25] Ethan Chen: In Private, is that exporter something we run as a pod?

[08:28] Markus Klein: Exactly. It’s part of the stack. You configure destination URL, auth tokens/keys, and it ships.

[08:37] Miguel Santos: Delivery semantics: at-least-once vs exactly-once. I’m asking because duplicates destroy correlation rules.

[08:45] Kevin Osei: It’s at-least-once. During retries you can see duplicates. We provide event_id so you can dedupe downstream. For Splunk specifically, you can use event_id as the unique key in your ingestion pipeline. Some folks use a KV store or transform; others dedupe in detection rules.

[09:06] Miguel Santos: Do you guarantee event_id uniqueness?

[09:10] Kevin Osei: Yes. It’s generated as a ULID/UUID style unique ID per event. We’ll confirm which one in the doc; but the key point is globally unique.

[09:21] Dana Whitfield: If you’re at-least-once, what about ordering? Like do I get role update after role create always?

[09:29] Kevin Osei: No strict ordering guarantee across distributed services. You get occurred_at timestamp plus received_at. For investigations, correlation IDs matter more.

[09:41] Miguel Santos: Okay. What’s your buffering behavior if Splunk HEC is down for, say, two hours?

[09:47] Markus Klein: The exporter buffers to disk up to a limit. There’s backpressure. We don’t block admin workflows—those still succeed—but you’ll see exporter alerts. After the destination comes back, it drains.

[10:07] Dana Whitfield: So events can be dropped if buffer limit is hit.

[10:11] Kevin Osei: Yes, worst case. We emit metrics for drop rate and latency. In private, you can scale exporter or increase buffer. We’ll give recommended sizing.

[10:24] Priya Desai: Is that documented? We’ll need that for our risk assessment.

[10:28] Naomi Feldman: We have runbook guidance and an SLO proposal for delivery latency and drop rate. We can share a summarized version.

[10:40] Miguel Santos: Field normalization for SIEM. Splunk wants “sourcetype” and sometimes nested JSON is annoying. Are you flattening fields?

[10:50] Kevin Osei: We keep stable top-level fields and then have namespaced extensions. In the exporter, we can output JSON event as-is, or we can map to Splunk-friendly keys. Usually customers keep JSON and define field extractions on event_type, actor_email, tenant_id.

[11:10] Miguel Santos: Sentinel is worse with nested JSON.

[11:13] Kevin Osei: Yeah. For Sentinel we recommend a flattened mapping at export time: event_type, event_id, occurred_at, actor_email, source_ip, tenant_id, resource_id, plus raw_json in a field. Again, we can send examples.

[11:33] Dana Whitfield: What about secrets and PII. We had another vendor log API keys in audit events.

[11:39] Naomi Feldman: We don’t log secret material. For API key events, we log key_id and metadata like name, created_by, scopes, but not the key value. We also have lint rules to prevent token-like strings. If something looks like “sk-…” we block.

[12:00] Miguel Santos: Do you log prompts? Like content.

[12:03] Naomi Feldman: Not in audit logs. Audit logs are for admin and security-relevant operations, not inference payloads.

[12:10] Ethan Chen: And do audit logs ever include customer end-user identifiers?

[12:15] Naomi Feldman: Only if you put them into resource names yourselves. We discourage that. Fields are classified and we avoid free-form values. Most IDs are opaque.

[12:27] Dana Whitfield: Okay. Private parity again: we need assurance that what happens in console is mirrored. Like if we change retention policy in the UI, do we get an audit event in private.

[12:38] Markus Klein: Yes, because console calls the same control plane APIs. The key is making sure every endpoint is instrumented.

[12:47] Naomi Feldman: And we’re adding regression tests that execute the sensitive action and assert an audit event shows up.

[12:57] Miguel Santos: Great. Can we get the list of event types? Like a catalog.

[13:02] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We’ll send the taxonomy list and required fields per type.

[13:10] Priya Desai: And control mapping. We’re SOC 2 and ISO 27001 aligned. We need evidence statements like “audit logs capture admin actions including RBAC changes and export config changes.”

[13:23] Naomi Feldman: We have an internal mapping doc. We can share an external-friendly excerpt and guidance on what evidence to collect in Private (screenshots, queries).

[13:36] Dana Whitfield: Please don’t send a 60-page thing. Just answer the questionnaire.

[13:40] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah, we’ll keep it tight.

[13:43] Miguel Santos: Can I drill on one thing: quota overrides / policy changes. If someone in Redwood—or in our org—changes routing policy, does that emit an event with the old value and new value?

[13:56] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy changes emit an event with a bounded diff summary. We don’t dump the entire policy doc if it’s huge; we’ll include the changed keys and before/after snippets.

[14:12] Miguel Santos: Bounded as in character limit?

[14:15] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We have cardinality budgets and size caps. Otherwise Splunk costs get wild.

[14:25] Dana Whitfield: What about model enable/disable actions? That’s sensitive for us.

[14:30] Naomi Feldman: Yes, runtime-level config changes that affect model availability are in-scope. We call them “fleet” or “model serving config” changes. Event taxonomy includes them.

[14:45] Ethan Chen: If a service changes config via automation, actor_type would be service, but can you tie to a CI pipeline or user?

[14:54] Markus Klein: If it comes through an authenticated API call, we can attribute to the service principal and include an auth_subject. If your automation uses a user token, it’s the user. For CI, we can include a “actor_display_name” like “github-actions” but it’s only as strong as your auth model.

[15:15] Miguel Santos: Okay. And export config changes themselves—if someone changes the Splunk endpoint or token, is that audited?

[15:22] Kevin Osei: Yes. Export destination create/update/delete is audited. Tokens are never logged; we log that it changed, not the value.

[15:34] Dana Whitfield: Awesome. One more: do you support syslog?

[15:38] Kevin Osei: Not as a first-class target today. Most folks do HTTPS or ship to an agent that forwards. We can do generic HTTP, and you can adapt to syslog via a relay.

[15:52] Miguel Santos: Fine.

[15:55] Liam O'Rourke: Can we talk about timelines? You’re in procurement now.

[16:00] Dana Whitfield: We’re trying to finish by end of month. But audit logs are gating.

[16:07] Naomi Feldman: Understood. The schema and exporter docs we can provide right away. For parity, the big items are already in progress; if there are specific event types you want confirmed for Private, list them and we’ll confirm status.

[16:23] Dana Whitfield: I’ll send a short list: RBAC change, API key rotate/revoke, retention/residency config, export config change, and private upgrade/rollback.

[16:34] Markus Klein: Great list.

[16:36] Miguel Santos: And please include source_ip and request_id in the sample events.

[16:42] Kevin Osei: Will do.

[16:44] Priya Desai: Also retention settings—be explicit what’s default vs configurable.

[16:50] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[16:52] (crosstalk)

[16:55] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else you want to hit today?

[16:59] Miguel Santos: Dedupe: In Splunk, do you recommend we dedupe on event_id at search time, or do something at ingestion?

[17:08] Kevin Osei: Ingestion dedupe is best if you can. Search-time dedupe can hide issues. But at minimum, your correlation logic should handle duplicates. We’ll include recommended patterns.

[17:23] Miguel Santos: Okay. And what about clock skew? occurred_at based on what?

[17:28] Kevin Osei: occurred_at is produced by the service that performed the action. In Private, if NTP is off, it’ll be off. We also include received_at at the exporter/ingestion side.

[17:43] Ethan Chen: That’s fair.

[17:45] Dana Whitfield: Cool. Can we get access to a sample dashboard or metrics for exporter drop rate?

[17:52] Markus Klein: In Private you can expose Prometheus metrics. We’ll share the metric names and alerts.

[18:01] Priya Desai: That’s helpful for evidence.

[18:04] Liam O'Rourke: Alright. I’ll recap and then we’ll get out.

[18:08] Liam O'Rourke: Naomi and Kevin will send the schema v1 and taxonomy and redaction notes. Kevin will send Splunk HEC and Sentinel config examples. Markus will send sample events for the five workflows, with source_ip and request_id. Dana and Miguel will confirm ingestion preferences and any required field mapping.

[18:30] Dana Whitfield: Sounds good.

[18:31] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[18:33] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[18:34] Naomi Feldman: Thanks everyone.

[18:36] Kevin Osei: Thanks.

[18:37] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[18:40] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll follow up by early next week. Bye.

(Note: Transcript continues with a few minutes of scheduling chatter and call wrap; omitted by Fireflies due to low audio confidence.)
